crockpot_turn_off.description: Stop the Crock-Pot and clear its timer.
crockpot_turn_off.notes: The one Crock-Pot write with no read-back: off takes no cook time with it, so this is sendable from a cold start.

crockpot_turn_on.description: Start the Crock-Pot on HIGH, keeping whatever cook time it already holds. This is what a bare 'on' means for a device with no single on state; the Cook Mode select is the control that reaches Warm and Low.
crockpot_turn_on.notes: HIGH rather than LOW because that is the mapping pywemo's on() uses; it is a convention, not something the device states.

time.description: As set_cook_mode.time — read it back and send it along. No default, for the same reason stated there: fail the write rather than start the cooker with a timer this command just invented.

plug_turn_off.description: Open the relay on a Wemo plug, switch or outdoor plug.

plug_turn_on.description: Close the relay on a Wemo plug, switch or outdoor plug.

returns.description: Echoes the new state, or the string 'Error' when the device was already in it. 'Error' here is not a failure worth surfacing — pywemo ignores it — but it does mean the reply cannot be used as a state reading.
returns.name: BinaryState

set_cook_mode.description: Set the Crock-Pot's cooking mode, carrying the cook time along unchanged.
set_cook_mode.example_notes: Low for four hours, built from mode=51 and time=240. Note the argument names are lowercase where BinaryState is not; they are spelled here exactly as they go on the wire.

time.description: SetCrockpotState carries BOTH values on every call, so changing the mode alone still means sending the cook time back with it — omit it and you have also cleared the timer. Read `time` from GetCrockpotState immediately before the write and send what it returned, which is what pywemo does.
time.notes: NO default, deliberately. A `source` parameter with no default is this spec saying the read-back is part of the send: a renderer that reaches this parameter with no value must FAIL the write, visibly, rather than substitute anything. pywemo falls back to 0 here, but what the appliance does with a 0 cook time in a heating mode is not verified, and "the write failed, try again" is a better outcome than a silently cleared timer. A client that genuinely cannot read the device (mid-provisioning, say) should ask the user for a time.

set_cook_time.description: Set the Crock-Pot's cook time in minutes, leaving the mode as it is.

mode.description: The mirror of the same trap: the action carries both values, so setting a time means sending the current mode back with it. Read it from GetCrockpotState first.
mode.notes: NO default, and this one earlier carried `default: 0` on the theory that off is harmless. It is not: the user adjusting the cook time almost certainly has a cooker that is RUNNING, and a failed read-back quietly substituting 0 would stop it mid-cook — dinner off, nothing on screen saying so. A missing value must fail the write instead.

setup_connect_home_network.description: Hand the device its home network credentials, over its setup AP. One step of the device.setup flow — which is also where the rule lives that this is sent TWICE, about 100ms apart, and that the outcome comes from polling GetNetworkStatus rather than from this reply.

auth.description: Auth mode from the chosen ApList entry, verbatim — the device rejects vocabulary that is not its own. OPEN for an open network.

encrypt.description: Cipher from the ApList entry (AES, TKIPAES); NONE for open.

password.description: The ENCRYPTED passphrase blob built per device.setup.methods[].softap.credential_encryption — never the plaintext. The empty string for an open network.

ssid.description: Target network SSID, exactly as GetApList reported it.

returns.description: Acknowledgement that the request was accepted, not the join result.
returns.name: PairingStatus

setup_resetup.description: Push a provisioned device back into setup mode over the LAN, without a physical factory reset. See device.setup.rejoin for when this is the right move and what state it leaves the device in on failure.

reset.description: Scope of the reset. No default, deliberately: every value is destructive to something, so a renderer reaching this parameter without a value must fail rather than pick a scope.

returns.description: 'success', or 'reset_remote' on at least one device — both mean it worked.
returns.name: Reset

match.description: ssdp:all is among the search targets, so every UPnP responder on the LAN answers. Keep only Belkin devices.
match.rule: Case-insensitively match 'belkin' or 'wemo' in any of: the USN header, the ST header, deviceType or manufacturer from the fetched description. The manufacturer element reads exactly 'Belkin International Inc.' on every device seen so far.

ssdp.port_fallback_notes: Wemo HTTP ports move across this range after a power cycle, so the port is never identity. When a cached LOCATION stops answering, probe this list in order for /setup.xml on the same host before concluding the device is gone.

request.example:
M-SEARCH * HTTP/1.1
HOST: 239.255.255.250:1900
MAN: "ssdp:discover"
MX: 2
ST: urn:Belkin:service:basicevent:1
request.mx_notes: pywemo sends MX 1, and the identification.ssdp.headers block above shows that value. This request block shows 2 because the repo's own verification scaffolding (scripts/wemo_discover.py) uses 2 and scripts/test_wemo_scaffolding.py parity-pins this field to it. Both are legal SSDP — MX is only the device's upper bound on how long it may delay its reply.
request.template_notes: Lines are CRLF-terminated and the request ends with a blank line (a trailing CRLF after the ST header). MAN's value includes the literal double quotes. Send one datagram per search target and collect unicast replies on the same socket.

response.dedupe_notes: Every search target is sent separately, so one device answers several times. Deduplicate on the LOCATION URL before fetching.
response.example:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
CACHE-CONTROL: max-age=86400
LOCATION: http://192.168.1.42:49153/setup.xml
ST: urn:Belkin:service:basicevent:1
USN: uuid:Socket-1_0-221517K0101769::urn:Belkin:service:basicevent:1
response.format: HTTP/1.1 200 OK status line followed by headers; no body.

headers_used.LOCATION: URL of the device description, normally http://<ip>:<port>/setup.xml
headers_used.ST: Search target echoed by the device
headers_used.USN: UDN plus the matching search target

parse_rules:
The document root is <root> in the UPnP namespace urn:schemas-upnp-org:device-1-0, with the device as <root><device>. Some firmware serves it with no namespace at all, so match on local element names rather than requiring the namespace.
Standard UPnP child elements of <device>: deviceType, friendlyName, manufacturer, manufacturerURL, modelDescription, modelName, modelNumber, modelURL, serialNumber, UDN, UPC, macAddress, iconList, serviceList, deviceList, presentationURL.
Any OTHER child element of <device> is a Belkin extension. Collect them into a map; firmwareVersion, rtos, iot, binaryOption and new_algo appear there, and rtos/iot select the setup encryption variant (see device.setup).
serviceList contains one <service> per entry; take serviceType, controlURL, eventSubURL and SCPDURL from each. Never hardcode a controlURL — the spelling varies across firmware generations.

timing.response_wait_notes: Matches pywemo's DISCOVER_TIMEOUT, which bounds the whole scan. MX is the device's own upper bound on how long it may delay its reply, so the listen window must be at least MX.
timing.timeout_source: Port probing matches pywemo's REQUESTS_TIMEOUT (10 s), which pywemo also uses for the HTTP fetch. The fetch timeout here stays at 5 s because the repo's verification scaffolding (scripts/wemo_discover.py) uses 5 and scripts/test_wemo_scaffolding.py parity-pins this field.

discovery_order: Read LOCATION from each unicast SSDP response.
Parse deviceType, UDN, friendlyName, serialNumber, macAddress, and serviceList.
Match variant by deviceType first and UDN prefix second.
Use each service controlURL from setup.xml for SOAP calls.

response_headers.st: Search target echoed by the device

device.name: Belkin Wemo Smart Devices
device.notes:
ALL Wemo devices are discovered via SSDP (Simple Service Discovery Protocol). NO static IP configuration is needed. Send an M-SEARCH to 239.255.255.250:1900 with ST matching a device or service search target, then fetch and parse setup.xml at the LOCATION URL to get the control URL, UDN, friendly name, serial/MAC metadata, service list, and deviceType.
Discovery order: 1. SSDP M-SEARCH; 2. parse LOCATION /setup.xml; 3. match deviceType and UDN prefix to a variant; 4. call SOAP actions at the service controlURL from setup.xml. Device ordering should use stable identity first: UDN, then serialNumber, then macAddress, with friendlyName used only as user-facing display text.
Port instability: Wemo Mini and related devices may change HTTP ports after a power cycle or reconnect. Always rediscover with SSDP or probe ports 49152-49159 in the pywemo order recorded below.
CONFIDENCE: SSDP discovery and SOAP action values HIGH (verified by pywemo, Home Assistant, ouimeaux lineage, and APK decompilation). Per-device command mappings MEDIUM; verified against public libraries but not validated via live capture for every appliance class.
Post-shutdown status: Belkin ended Wemo support on 2026-01-31 (app, remote access, voice integrations and firmware updates all dead). Only the Thread-based WLS0503, WSC010 and WSP100 plus the WDC010 doorbell remain supported; any HomeKit-configured Wemo (WLS0403, WDS060, WSP080 among them) keeps working through HomeKit. Local SSDP/SOAP discovery, provisioning and control are unaffected, and pywemo remains actively maintained.

credentials.notes: No token or certificate is issued to the client: post-setup control is unauthenticated SOAP to anyone on the LAN. Treat network segmentation, not device auth, as the security control for Wemo hardware. Published advisories on these exact surfaces underline that: CVE-2023-27217 (unauthenticated stack overflow in basicevent#ChangeFriendlyName on the F7C063 Mini, unpatched — Belkin declined as EOL), CVE-2023-33768 (WSP080 firmware-signature verification flaw enabling DoS via crafted firmware) and CVE-2018-6692 (Insight RCE via libUPnPHndlr.so).

factory_reset.effect: Clears the stored WiFi credentials, friendly name, rules/timers and any cloud/account association, and returns the device to setup mode. The UDN, serial number and MAC address are hardware identity and survive a reset, so a device keeps its stable discovery keys across reprovisioning.
factory_reset.notes: Hold times are vendor-documented and vary by generation; treat them as a starting point and watch the LED rather than the clock. The reliable confirmation that a reset worked is the reappearance of the open Wemo.* setup AP.

procedures.basis: Belkin's published Wemo user guides for the plug-style models. Not replayed against hardware here.
procedures.indicator: Status LED blinks, then the device reboots into setup mode and starts advertising its Wemo.* AP.
procedures.name: Restore button held while power is applied (plug-style devices)

steps.action: Unplug the device from the outlet.
Press and hold the Restore button, then plug the device back in while still holding.
Keep holding for about 5 seconds after power is applied, then release.
Wait up to 90 seconds for the device to finish rebooting.
steps.expect: An open Wemo.* network appears in the client's WiFi scan.

procedures.basis: Belkin's published Wemo user guides for the in-wall switch and dimmer models. Not replayed against hardware here.
procedures.indicator: Status LED cycles, then the device reboots into setup mode.
procedures.name: Restore button held on a mains-powered in-wall device

steps.action: Leave the switch powered at the breaker.
Press and hold the Restore button on the device body for about 10 seconds until the LED changes pattern.
steps.notes: In-wall units cannot be reset by cycling power at the breaker alone; the button must be held.

steps.action: Wait up to 90 seconds for the device to reboot into setup mode.

methods.description: Join the device's own setup AP and drive the WiFiSetup SOAP service. This is the only known way to give a Wemo device WiFi credentials without the (now defunct) Belkin app.

ApList.description: WiFiSetup#GetApList returns a single ApList value holding the device's scan results, newline-separated.
ApList.open_network_handling: When the selected entry's cipher is NONE, skip the encryption entirely: send auth=OPEN, encrypt=NONE and an empty password string. Do not call GetMetaInfo — no key material is needed.
parse_rules: Split on newline. SKIP THE FIRST LINE — it is a header/count, not an access point.
Strip whitespace and any trailing comma from each remaining line.
Ignore lines with no '|' — some firmware emits blank or partial trailing lines.
Split on '|'. Column 0 is the SSID. Column 1 is the channel.
The LAST column is 'AUTHMODE/CIPHER'. Split it on '/' to get the `auth` and `encrypt` arguments for ConnectHomeNetwork. Do not assume a fixed column index for it; the number of columns varies.
Send the device's own strings back verbatim. A network the device can see is still rejected if the auth string does not match its own vocabulary.

unsupported_marker.meaning: The device cannot express that network's security mode and will never join it. WPA3 appears this way. The remedy is a WPA2 compatibility SSID for the duration of setup, not a retry.

MetaInfo.description: metainfo#GetMetaInfo returns a single MetaInfo value: a pipe-delimited string of at least six fields. Field order matters — using the serial where the MAC belongs yields a valid-looking blob the device rejects without explanation.

fields.description: 12 hex characters, no separators. Key material.
fields.name: mac

fields.description: Device serial. Key material.
fields.name: serial_number

fields.description: Regional SKU, e.g. Wemo_WW.
fields.name: device_sku

fields.description: The device's own setup AP name — it tells you what it advertises.
fields.name: access_point_ssid

fields.description: e.g. Socket.
fields.name: model_name

algorithm_steps: 1. Choose the keydata layout for this device (see variants below).
2. salt = the first 8 characters of keydata, as UTF-8 bytes (NOT hex-decoded).
3. iv = the first 16 characters of keydata, as UTF-8 bytes (NOT hex-decoded).
4. aes_key = MD5(utf8(keydata) || salt)[0:16]. One MD5 round only; do not iterate.
5. Pad the UTF-8 passphrase with PKCS#7 to a multiple of 16 bytes.
6. Encrypt with AES-128-CBC using aes_key and iv.
7. Base64-encode the ciphertext (standard alphabet, with '=' padding).

8. If this variant sets add_lengths, append four lowercase hex digits: the length of the base64 string from step 7, then the length of the plaintext passphrase, EACH zero-padded to exactly two digits. A passphrase of 8 characters contributes '08', not '8'.
9. Send the result as the `password` argument of ConnectHomeNetwork.
credential_encryption.encoding: base64 of the ciphertext, then — for methods 1 and 3 only — four hex digits: the length of that base64 string and the length of the plaintext passphrase, each zero-padded to exactly two digits. Note that OpenSSL 1.x prefixes ciphertext with a 16-byte "Salted__"+salt header even when the salt is given explicitly while OpenSSL 3.x does not, so strip that header conditionally.
credential_encryption.key_derivation: Key material ("keydata") is assembled from the MetaInfo string returned by metainfo#GetMetaInfo, split on '|', where field 0 is the MAC and field 1 is the serial number. The AES key is MD5(keydata_bytes + salt_bytes) truncated to 16 bytes, with salt = keydata[0:8] and iv = keydata[0:16] — equivalent to OpenSSL's legacy EVP_BytesToKey MD5 derivation for AES-128 with the IV supplied explicitly.
credential_encryption.notes: The scheme protects the passphrase from a passive listener on the open setup AP, but the key is derived entirely from device metadata that the device hands out unauthenticated, so it is obfuscation rather than a trust boundary. Passphrases shorter than 8 characters are rejected by the device (network status 2).

openssl_equivalent.command: openssl enc -aes-128-cbc -md md5 -S <hex of salt bytes> -iv <hex of iv bytes> -pass pass:<keydata>
openssl_equivalent.notes: Produces byte-identical output to the steps above. Note the header quirk: OpenSSL 1.x prefixes its output with the 16-byte "Salted__" + salt header even when the salt is supplied with -S, while OpenSSL 3.x does not. Strip that header only when it is actually present — slicing 16 bytes unconditionally, as older published scripts do, silently corrupts the credential on OpenSSL 3.x.

password_constraints.notes: A passphrase under 8 characters is rejected by the device with network status 2. The upper bound follows from the two-hex-digit length suffix: both the plaintext and the base64 ciphertext must be 255 characters or fewer.

test_vectors.description: Reproducible vectors so an implementation can be verified without hardware. The MAC is from the IANA documentation range (00:00:5E) and the serial is invented — these identify no real device. Every value below is generated from the algorithm_steps above. scripts/test_wemo_spec.py transcribes those steps using only hashlib, base64 and openssl — importing none of this project's code — and asserts the transcription reproduces these vectors, so the published algorithm cannot quietly rot.

vectors.suffix_explanation: Same lengths as method 1; only the keydata layout differs.

variants.selector: setup.xml contains rtos=1 and not iot=1.
The Wemo app associates this with binaryOption=1, but pywemo reports the rtos/iot selector above matches hardware more often. Try this variant manually if the others fail.

softap.port_notes: Probe rather than assume: the setup-mode port varies like the normal one. pywemo walks the same fallback list it uses on the LAN.

steps.action: Factory reset the device (or call basicevent#ReSetup on a provisioned one) so it re-enters setup mode.
steps.expect: Device starts advertising an open Wemo.* WiFi network.

steps.action: Join the device's setup AP from the provisioning client.
steps.expect: Client receives a 10.22.22.x address with 10.22.22.1 as gateway.

steps.action: Fetch the device description and resolve service control URLs.
steps.expect: serviceList contains urn:Belkin:service:WiFiSetup:1 and urn:Belkin:service:metainfo:1. Belkin also adds non-standard elements alongside the UPnP ones — rtos, iot, binaryOption, new_algo, firmwareVersion — and these select the passphrase encryption variant (see credential_encryption.variants).

steps.action: Read device metadata used to derive the passphrase encryption key.
steps.expect: MetaInfo pipe-delimited string; fields 0 and 1 supply the key material.

steps.action: Ask the device to scan for nearby access points.
steps.expect: ApList string. The first line is a header and is skipped. Each remaining line is pipe-delimited with SSID in column 0, channel in column 1, and 'AUTHMODE/CIPHER' in the last column; a trailing comma is common. An auth mode of 'Unknown' means the device cannot join that network (WPA3 appears this way). Supported ciphers are NONE, AES and TKIPAES.

response_fields.description: Newline-separated scan results; see payload_formats.ApList above.
response_fields.name: ApList

steps.action: Encrypt the home network passphrase and hand the device its credentials.
steps.expect: Returns PairingStatus. Send this action twice about 100ms apart — pywemo reports a markedly higher success rate when it is repeated, for reasons that are not understood. For an open network send auth=OPEN, encrypt=NONE and an empty password.

arguments.description: Target network SSID, exactly as reported by GetApList.
arguments.name: ssid

arguments.description: Auth mode from the ApList entry, e.g. WPA2PSK.
arguments.name: auth

arguments.description: Cipher from the ApList entry, e.g. AES.
arguments.name: encrypt

response_fields.description: Acknowledgement that the request was accepted, not the join result. The outcome comes from polling GetNetworkStatus.
response_fields.name: PairingStatus

steps.action: Poll the join result until the device reports a connected state.
steps.expect: NetworkStatus: 0 = still connecting, 1 = connected, 2 = rejected because the passphrase is shorter than 8 characters, 3 = handshaking (usually becomes 1 within a few seconds, so do not treat it as a failure).

status_codes.0: Still trying to connect. Keep polling.
status_codes.2: Rejected — passphrase shorter than 8 characters. Terminal failure; retrying will not help.
status_codes.3: Handshaking. Usually becomes 1 within a few seconds; not a failure.

steps.action: Close setup mode so the device leaves its AP and joins the home network.
steps.expect: Returns status = success. Follow with basicevent#SetSetupDoneStatus where present; it is absent on some firmware and its absence is not an error. Setup AP disappears and the client can rejoin its normal network.

steps.action: Rediscover the device on the home LAN by SSDP and confirm control.
steps.expect: Device answers with a LOCATION URL; basicevent#GetBinaryState succeeds.

timing.connect_send_notes: Send ConnectHomeNetwork twice about 100ms apart. pywemo reports a markedly higher success rate when it is repeated; the reason is not understood, but it is cheap and harmless.
timing.notes: Devices routinely take 10-15 seconds to join, so a poll timeout below 20 seconds produces false failures; pywemo's setup timeout defaults to 20 s and it enforces a 20 s floor. Status 3 usually flips to 1 within a few more seconds — wait rather than retrying.

causes: Target SSID is 5 GHz. Every Wemo radio is 2.4 GHz only, and a band-steering router advertising one SSID on both bands is the most common cause of an unexplained failure.

Wrong encryption variant. Sweep all six combinations of method (1, 2, 3) and add_lengths (true, false), in this order: (1, true), (2, false), (3, true), (1, false), (2, true), (3, false). The first three are the documented pairings; the last three are unlikely but cheap to try.
Weak signal. Some units need a strong signal to complete setup even though they run fine on a weak one afterwards.
troubleshooting.symptom: ConnectHomeNetwork accepted but NetworkStatus never reaches 1.

causes: Passphrase is shorter than 8 characters. Terminal — retrying will not help.
Handshaking. Wait a few more seconds; 3 usually precedes 1. Not a failure.
The device cannot express that security mode; WPA3 is the usual cause. Add a WPA2 SSID for the duration of setup.
troubleshooting.symptom: Target network reports auth mode Unknown in ApList.

causes: On plug-style devices the Restore button must be held THROUGH power-on; pressing it on a running device does nothing. Watch the LED rather than timing the hold.
troubleshooting.symptom: Device is not advertising a Wemo.* AP after a reset.

causes: The client fell back to cellular or another interface. Pin the route to 10.22.22.0/24.
Wrong port. Probe the port_probe_list rather than assuming 49153.
troubleshooting.symptom: Setup AP is joinable but HTTP times out.

causes: Genuinely try again — pywemo's own documentation lists this first. Wemo devices sometimes fail to connect and the identical sequence subsequently works.
troubleshooting.symptom: Everything fails repeatedly for no clear reason.

setup.notes:
Wemo devices ship unprovisioned and cannot be discovered by SSDP until they hold WiFi credentials. Provisioning is entirely local: the device hosts an open setup AP and accepts the home network credentials over the same SOAP 1.1 stack used for normal control. The Belkin cloud is not required at any point, which is why Wemo hardware remains recoverable after the January 2026 cloud shutdown.
CONFIDENCE: HIGH. Service names, action names, argument names, the ApList layout, the network status codes and all three passphrase encryption variants come from pywemo's implementation (pywemo/ouimeaux_device/__init__.py, Apache 2.0), which is maintained and exercised against real hardware across several device generations. Not yet replayed against hardware by this project.
Always read the WiFiSetup controlURL from setup.xml rather than assuming a path: both /upnp/control/WiFiSetup1 and /upnp/control/wifi1 have been reported across firmware generations.

rejoin.notes: A provisioned Wemo device can be pushed back into setup mode over the LAN with basicevent#ReSetup, which avoids a physical factory reset when the device is still reachable on the old network — useful when the router is being replaced but the device is not. If the old network is already gone, the device is unreachable and a physical factory reset is the only path. Note that ReSetup clears the stored credentials, so a failed reprovisioning leaves the device in setup mode, not on the old network.

steps.action: While the device is still reachable on the old network, send basicevent#ReSetup.
steps.expect: Returns Reset = success; at least one device reports reset_remote instead and still resets correctly. Device drops off the LAN and starts advertising its Wemo.* setup AP.

arguments.description: Scope of the reset: 1 clears name/icon/rules ("Clear Personalized Info"), 2 clears everything including WiFi ("Factory Restore"), 5 clears WiFi credentials only ("Change Wi-Fi"). Codes were consistent across the devices pywemo has been tested against but are not guaranteed for every model.
arguments.name: Reset

response_fields.description: 'success', or 'reset_remote' on at least one device.
response_fields.name: Reset

steps.action: Run the softap_soap provisioning flow against the new network.

testing.notes: Key facts checked against first-party captures of real hardware (research store: wemo-devices/captures/, ten models incl. Insight, Maker, Dimmer, Crock-Pot setup). No flow has been driven end-to-end from this spec by this project.

characteristics:
Basic on/off smart plug.
Some firmware and APK mocks identify the Mini as socket:1.
On/off is basicevent GetBinaryState/SetBinaryState; the control surface is declared in the top-level `commands` and `entities` blocks.
This is the model whose HTTP port moves after a power cycle. The port is not identity — rediscover by SSDP or probe identification.port_probe_list before deciding the plug is gone.
basicevent#ChangeFriendlyName on this model is CVE-2023-27217, an unauthenticated stack overflow Belkin declined to patch as EOL. A client has no reason to send it and every reason not to expose it.

variants.alternate_models_notes: F7C045 is Belkin's part number for the same appliance ("Crock-Pot Smart Slow Cooker with Wemo"); SCCPWM600 is Jarden's. A user reading a support article and a user reading the base of their cooker are holding the same device.
characteristics:
Cooking modes are off=0, warm=50, low=51, high=52 (payload_formats.CrockpotMode).
BinaryState IS NOT THIS DEVICE'S STATE. basicevent#GetBinaryState answers 0 whatever the cooker is doing, so on/off comes from `mode != 0` in GetCrockpotState. This is the one Wemo where the universal switch surface is present and lies.
Mode and cook time are set together by one action; there is no set-the-mode-alone call. See commands.set_cook_mode.
SetCrockpotState is acknowledged, not confirmed. pywemo re-reads the state after every write because the cooker does not always take the setting.
Control surface is declared in the top-level `commands` and `entities` blocks.

identification.udn_prefix_notes: Spelled exactly as the device sends it: capital C, lowercase p. pywemo dispatches on `udn.startswith("uuid:Crockpot")`, which is case-SENSITIVE, and our own notes have carried a lowercase "uuid:crockpot-1_0-..." guess elsewhere. Match case-insensitively and you cannot be wrong either way.

entities.name: Plug
entities.notes: `on_when: nonzero` rather than a comparison against 1, because an Insight reports 8 for "on, and the attached load is idling". Treating 8 as anything but on gives a plug that reads as off while it is powering something. The reading needs the split rule in payload_formats.BinaryState: some firmware answers with the long pipe-delimited form and only field 0 is the state.

entities.name: Slow Cooker
entities.notes: Reads `mode`, NOT BinaryState. basicevent#GetBinaryState answers 0 on this device whatever it is doing — pywemo overrides its own base implementation for exactly that reason — so the obvious binding, the one every other Wemo switch uses, yields a Crock-Pot that is permanently off and a toggle that springs back. `turn_on` selects HIGH and keeps the cook time; Warm and Low are reachable through the Cook Mode select.

entities.name: Cook Mode
entities.notes: The mode codes are also in payload_formats.CrockpotMode, which is where a parser should read them; the table is repeated here in the shape the entity layer already uses for a select (ember-mug spells its temperature unit the same way) because a consumer that reads entities and nothing else still has to render a label rather than the number 51. A value outside the table is a mode we do not know: show it as unknown rather than folding it into `off`. `select_option` is the one role name in this file that no consumer resolves yet — it is the parameterised form the action actually has, where the catalogue's other selects declare one command per option.

entities.name: Cook Time
entities.notes: No `max`: the longest cook time the appliance accepts is not something we have established, and inventing a bound would either forbid a setting the device allows or promise one it rejects. A consumer needing a slider range should pick its own and say it is its own. Writing this sends the current mode back alongside the new time — see commands.set_cook_time.

entities.name: Cooked Time
entities.notes: Minutes elapsed in the current run, counting up, where Cook Time counts down. One GetCrockpotState call serves this, Cook Mode, Cook Time and the switch — poll once and fan the three values out rather than calling per entity.

BinaryState.description: Relay/light state, returned by basicevent#GetBinaryState and accepted by SetBinaryState.

fields.description: The state itself, and the only documented field of the long form. Declared as a delimited field rather than left to the parse rule below because a decoder cannot follow prose: this is what says the value may need splitting before any of `values` applies.
fields.name: state

parse_rules:
Some firmware returns extra pipe-delimited values after the state (for example on dimmers). Split on '|' and take field 0 rather than parsing the whole string as an integer.
The trailing fields of the long form are NOT InsightParams and must not be read with that layout: the two differ in length and nothing published says the columns line up. Field 0 is the documented part. Reach for insight#GetInsightParams when you want the energy figures.

values.8: On, but the attached load is drawing standby-level power. Insight devices report this; treat it as ON for control purposes.

CrockpotMode.description: Cooking mode of the Crock-Pot Smart Slow Cooker: returned as the `mode` value of basicevent#GetCrockpotState, sent as the `mode` argument of basicevent#SetCrockpotState, and pushed as the `mode` event property. This is the Crock-Pot's state — BinaryState is not (see device.variants SCCPWM600-V1).
parse_rules:
The numbers are the device's own and are not an ordering: there is no mode between 0 and 50, and 51 is not "one more heat than" 50. Map through this table rather than treating the value as a level.
Any other value is a mode this table does not know. Keep the raw number and render it as unknown; mapping an unrecognised value to `off` would tell a user their cooker is off while it is heating. pywemo returns a distinct unknown (-1) for exactly this reason.
Off is a real mode, not the absence of one. A client deriving on/off from this field asks `mode != 0`, which is what pywemo does.

InsightParams.description: Energy and timing counters from insight#GetInsightParams, as a single pipe-delimited string.

fields.description: Current BinaryState — see the BinaryState format above.
fields.name: state

fields.description: Unix timestamp of the last state change.
fields.name: lastchange

fields.description: Seconds the load has been on during the current run.
fields.name: onfor_seconds

fields.description: Seconds on today.
fields.name: ontoday_seconds

fields.description: Seconds on over the measurement period.
fields.name: ontotal_seconds

fields.description: Length of the measurement period in seconds (commonly 1209600 = 14 days).
fields.name: timeperiod

fields.description: WiFi signal strength. Easy to miss — omitting this field shifts every power reading one column left, which reads as plausible but wrong data rather than as an error.
fields.name: wifipower

fields.description: Instantaneous power draw in milliwatts.
fields.name: currentpower_mw

fields.description: Energy used today, in milliwatt-minutes.
fields.name: todaymw

fields.description: Energy used over the measurement period, in milliwatt-minutes.
fields.name: totalmw

fields.description: Standby detection threshold in milliwatts.
fields.name: powerthreshold

parse_rules: Split on '|'. Fields are positional; there are no names on the wire.
Firmware may append fields beyond those documented here. Keep any extras rather than discarding them, and do not treat a longer string as a parse failure.

MetaInfo.description: Device metadata from metainfo#GetMetaInfo. Also used during setup — see device.setup for how fields 0 and 1 key the passphrase encryption.

fields.description: 12 hex characters, no separators.
fields.name: mac

fields.description: The device's own setup AP name.
fields.name: access_point_ssid

ouimeaux.role: Legacy Python Wemo implementation and pywemo lineage.

scheduling.applies_to_notes: Scoped to the switch family, by `device.variants` name, because that is where the evidence is: pywemo drives FetchRules/StoreRules against these classes, and the captured schedule row is an Insight's. `supported: true` unscoped would let a consumer advertise on-device scheduling for the Crock-Pot and the Holmes appliances, where whether the rules service honours anything is an open question below — and the Crock-Pot is doubly excluded because a rule's action sets the binary state, which is not that device's state at all. Outside this list, treat scheduling support as UNKNOWN rather than absent: the service may well be present, and finding out is listed in open_questions.
scheduling.client_side_alternative: A client that only needs "turn this on at 17:00" while it is running can simply send the ordinary control command at 17:00 and skip all of the above. That is the honest fallback, and its limitation is the whole reason the rules database is worth the trouble: close the app, or let the phone sleep, and the schedule does not happen.
scheduling.confidence_notes: MEDIUM, and the parts are not equally known. The transfer and the table schemas are HIGH — pywemo implements both against real hardware. The meaning of a schedule row's columns is inference from two known-good rows, one written by pywemo and one captured from a device configured by the Wemo app. `open_questions` below lists exactly what is not established; none of it has been replayed by this project.
scheduling.device_clock_dependency: Rules run on the device's own clock, so a device whose time is wrong runs the schedule wrong. Set it with timesync#TimeSync (UTC, %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S) before trusting a schedule, and remember that the Belkin cloud used to be what kept it right.
limitations:
A rule's action is a number — 1.0 on, 0.0 off, 2.0 toggle. There is no column that carries a Crock-Pot mode, so "start the cooker on Low at 17:00" does not appear to be expressible: what a rule can schedule is the BINARY state. On the Crock-Pot that is the surface which answers 0 whatever the device is doing, so a scheduled rule there is doubly suspect and must be tested on hardware before anybody relies on it to start cooking unattended.
The Crock-Pot's own cook time IS a device-run countdown and is not part of this at all: SetCrockpotState carries `time` in minutes and the appliance counts it down itself. That is the timer that certainly works today. It starts when you send it — it is a duration, not a start time.
Nothing here is a way to schedule from off-network. The device runs the rule; something must have written it while on the same LAN.
open_questions: DayID's encoding. The one captured schedule is named 'Nightly' and uses 1, and pywemo's non-schedule rule uses -1. Whether it is a bitmask, an enum or an index is not established, and a wrong guess means a rule that fires on the wrong day.
The full RULES.Type vocabulary. Only 'Time Interval' and 'Long Press' are attested; the app also offered sunrise/sunset and away modes.
Whether the appliance classes (Crock-Pot, coffee maker, humidifier) honour rules at all, and what StartAction means on one.
What CountdownTime does. The name suggests the app's 'turn off after N minutes' timer, but both observed rows carry 0.
Whether StoreRules validates anything. If it does not, a malformed database may leave the device with no working rules and no error.

storage.format: sqlite3, zipped, base64-encoded in the SOAP argument

columns.ruleId: text — note the string type and lowercase spelling, unlike RULES.RuleID.

BLOCKEDRULES.description: Rules the device is told to ignore.

LOCATIONINFO.description: Where the app said the device lives — sunrise/sunset rules needed it.

columns.CountdownTime: Present on every row, 0 on both observed ones. Purpose not established.
columns.DayID: Which day(s). See open_questions — the encoding is not established.
columns.EndAction: The same at EndTime; -1.0 where there is nothing to do.
columns.Level: -1 on both observed rows; presumably a dimmer level.
columns.StartAction: What happens at StartTime: 1.0 on, 0.0 off, 2.0 toggle.
columns.Type: An integer, distinct from RULES.Type. -1 on both observed rows.

RULEDEVICES.description: One row per device a rule acts on, carrying the timing.

columns.Name: Free text, shown in the app that no longer exists.
columns.RuleOrder: Evaluation order; use max(existing) + 1 for a new rule.
columns.Sync: 'NOSYNC'. Declared INTEGER in the schema and holding a string.
columns.Type: Rule kind. Two values are attested: 'Time Interval' (a schedule, from a device configured by the Wemo app) and 'Long Press' (what pywemo writes). Others certainly exist — the app offered sunset, sunrise and away modes — and are not documented here.

RULES.sentinel_dates: Those two dates are not dates. The same pair appears in a rule pywemo writes and in a rule the Wemo app wrote, which is what makes them constants meaning "no date restriction" rather than somebody's birthday. Copy them; do not compute them.

RULESNOTIFYMESSAGE.description: Notification text a rule used to push through the cloud.

columns.DeviceIndex: 0-based position within the rule's target list.

TARGETDEVICES.description: The devices a rule ACTS ON, where RULEDEVICES is the devices it listens to — a long-press rule on one switch targets others. A schedule targeting only its own device still gets no row here.

tables.tables_notes: All nine tables and their columns are transcribed from pywemo's rules-database ORM (pywemo/ouimeaux_device/api/rules_db.py), which both reads real devices' databases and CREATES the empty one when a device 404s the download — so this listing is sufficient to build that empty database, named 'temppluginRules.db' inside the zip. A schedule touches only RULES and RULEDEVICES; the rest exist so the device finds every table it expects. Column types beyond the ones annotated are unremarkable (SQLite is dynamically typed and pywemo declares TEXT/INTEGER as shown); the two standing oddities are RULES.Sync, declared INTEGER and holding the string 'NOSYNC', and BLOCKEDRULES.ruleId, a string where every other rule id is an integer.

scheduling.summary: Schedules live ON THE DEVICE, in a SQLite database it hands out and takes back over SOAP. A client fetches the database, edits rows, zips it, base64-encodes it and posts it back; the device then runs the schedule on its own clock with nothing else on the network. That is the property worth having — a phone app scheduling a future action has to still be running at the time, and on iOS it will not be.

transfer.description: The database moves whole, in both directions. There is no add-one-rule call in the pair a current client uses.

steps.action: Ask the device where its rules database is and which version it holds.

response_fields.description: Current version. The store call must send this plus one.
response_fields.name: ruleDbVersion

response_fields.description: URL on the device itself, to fetch over plain HTTP.
response_fields.name: ruleDbPath

steps.action: Download the database.
steps.expect: A ZIP archive containing one SQLite file. Keep the inner filename — it goes back unchanged, and a device that has never held a rule may 404 here, in which case create an empty database with the tables below and use the name 'temppluginRules.db'.

steps.action: Edit the rows.
steps.expect: FETCH, MODIFY, STORE — never construct a database from scratch for a device that already had one. The store replaces everything, so a client that builds a fresh database silently deletes every rule the user made in the Wemo app, and that app is gone: they cannot make them again.

steps.action: Send the database back.

arguments.description: The version FetchRules returned, plus one.
arguments.name: ruleDbVersion

arguments.description: 1 — apply the database rather than only storing it.
arguments.name: processDb

arguments.description: The zipped database, base64-encoded, wrapped in a CDATA section that is itself XML-ESCAPED — the argument's literal text begins '<![CDATA[' and ends ']]>'. That is not a typo carried forward: it is what the device accepts, and sending a real CDATA section instead is the obvious correction that does not work.
arguments.name: ruleDbBody

eventing.description: Wemo devices push state changes over standard UPnP eventing, to the eventSubURL each service publishes in setup.xml. This is the difference between a control that reacts when somebody presses the button on the device and one that only knows what it last wrote: a client that polls GetBinaryState every few seconds still misses the Crock-Pot finishing. Every field below is what pywemo's subscription registry sends and parses; none of it has been replayed against hardware here.

notify.description: The device POSTs an XML property set to the callback URL whenever a subscribed value changes. Each <e:property> holds exactly one child whose tag names the property and whose text is the new value — the same values the matching Get* action returns, in the same encoding, so one parser serves both paths.
notify.parse_rule: propertyset -> each property -> first child -> {child.tag: child.text}

BinaryState.notes: Sent by every switch-like device. Carries the pipe-delimited long form on some firmware, so split on '|' and take field 0 here too.

InsightParams.notes: Insight only. An Insight stops sending these when it is switched off, so a gap in the stream is not a lost subscription.

cookedTime.notes: Crock-Pot only. Minutes cooked so far in this run.

mode.notes: Crock-Pot only. The device's own state, whether it changed by SOAP or by the front-panel button.

renew.notes: A renewal carries SID and no CALLBACK/NT. A device that has forgotten the subscription answers with an error; the recovery is to UNSUBSCRIBE for safety and then subscribe afresh, which is also what a port change after a power cycle looks like from here.

eventing.subscribable_services_notes: Subscribe to the services a device actually publishes — take the eventSubURL from its own serviceList and skip the rest. On the plug and the Crock-Pot that is basicevent alone.

subscribe.header_notes: The angle brackets around CALLBACK's URL are part of the value, not notation. The client must already be listening on that address: the device connects back to it, so a client behind NAT or on a different subnet gets a subscription that never delivers. Pick the callback host by which local interface routes to the device rather than by whatever the OS calls primary.

response_headers.SID: Subscription identifier, needed to renew or cancel.
response_headers.TIMEOUT: Second-<n>, the lifetime the device actually granted.

subscribe.timeout_notes: TIMEOUT is a request, not a promise — renew on the value the device returns in its own TIMEOUT header, not on the one you asked for.

request_format.argument_qualification: CRITICAL: action arguments are UNQUALIFIED. Send <ssid>value</ssid>, not <u:ssid>value</u:ssid>. Only the action element itself carries the u: prefix, and the xmlns:u declaration belongs ON THE ACTION ELEMENT, not on the envelope. Several XML libraries (including Python's ElementTree) hoist namespace declarations to the root element, which is equivalent XML but not what these devices normally receive.
request_format.description: Everything needed to build a Wemo SOAP request byte for byte. Wemo firmware runs a minimal XML parser, so send this shape rather than whatever your XML library produces by default.
request_format.escaping: XML-escape argument values (&, <, >). An SSID containing an ampersand otherwise produces a malformed document. Note that pywemo does not escape, so this is a divergence in our favour rather than a documented device behaviour.

example.description: ConnectHomeNetwork as it goes on the wire.

response_format.description: Responses are a SOAP envelope whose Body has exactly one child, named <ActionName>Response. That element's direct children are the named return values; take their text content. A Body child named Fault is an error.

setup_related_actions.ReSetup: Takes a Reset argument selecting scope: 1 clears name/icon/rules, 2 factory resets, 5 clears WiFi credentials only. Returns Reset = success (or reset_remote on at least one device). See device.setup.rejoin.
setup_related_actions.SetSetupDoneStatus: Sent after a successful CloseSetup. Absent on some firmware; treat a SOAP fault or missing action as non-fatal.

RemoteAccess.description: Enables cloud remote access and returns the key material for it (statusCode 'S'/'F' plus homeId and per-phone private keys in the response blob). Dead end post-shutdown — documented so the service is recognisable in a serviceList, not because it still works.

remoteaccess.availability: Present in the Crock-Pot and Bridge SCPDs with SCPDURL /remoteaccess.xml. The app's in-argument list differs slightly by firmware generation (both orders recorded above).

rules.availability: The on-device automation store — where the (now dead) Wemo app kept its timers, schedules and long-press rules. FetchRules/StoreRules are the pair a current implementation uses; the longer list comes from a 2016 dump of the service description and is not what pywemo drives, so take the action list from the device's own SCPD rather than from here. See the top-level `scheduling` block for what the two actions move.

GetRegistrationData.description: Reads the device's cloud registration blob (returns pluginprivateKey, smartprivateKey, homeId and a statusCode).

GetRegistrationStatus.description: Poll after PairAndRegister. The app retries while RegistrationStatus is 'F' and StatusCode is 'RETRY', every 10 s for up to 60 s, before giving up on registration (the LAN join itself has already succeeded or failed by then).

PairAndRegister.description: One-shot provisioning + cloud registration: the in-args carry the WiFi credentials as PairingData XML (<PairingData><ssid><![CDATA[...]]></ssid><auth>..</auth><password>..</password><encrypt>..</encrypt><channel>..</channel></PairingData>, password encrypted exactly as for ConnectHomeNetwork) and the account binding as RegistrationData XML (<RegistrationData><DeviceId>..</DeviceId><DeviceName><![CDATA[...]]></DeviceName><SetupToken>..</SetupToken><GroupId>..</GroupId></RegistrationData>; a second layout swaps in <smartprivateKey> and <ReUnionKey>). The account half needs the defunct Belkin cloud, so post-shutdown provisioning uses WiFiSetup#ConnectHomeNetwork instead.

smartsetup.availability: Seen in real-hardware captures (pywemo VCR cassettes) alongside WiFiSetup:1 on the light switch, Maker, outdoor plug and humidifier. Action list and arguments above come from the Crock-Pot's own /smartsetup.xml SCPD (research store: wemo-devices/captures/ crockpot_setup_capture.yaml) and the Wemo app v1.30.2, whose setup flow drives exactly these three actions. Resolve the controlURL from setup.xml like any other service.

wifi_setup.availability: Present on the setup AP. Always resolve the controlURL from the serviceList in setup.xml; the path spelling differs across firmware generations.
